explanation: Cabrillo is the de facto standard plain-text file format that most contest sponsors require for electronic log submission: a defined header section (callsign, category, club, etc.) followed by one line per QSO recording frequency, mode, date/time, and exchange data, which lets contest-scoring software automatically cross-check thousands of submitted logs against each other. It's a post-contest log file format, not an over-the-air exchange protocol, a rulebook, or a real-time digital mode, so the other three choices misdescribe what it actually is.

question: Which of the following contacts may be confirmed through the Logbook of The World (LoTW)?
answers: Special event contacts between stations in the US
Contacts between a US station and a non-US station
Contacts for Worked All States credit
explanation: ARRL's Logbook of The World is a general-purpose contact-confirmation database: once both operators upload matching, cryptographically-signed QSO records, LoTW produces a confirmed match regardless of what award category that contact might later support — a domestic special-event contact, a US-to-DX contact, and a Worked-All-States-qualifying domestic contact are all processed identically by the system. Because none of those contact types are excluded, 'all of these' is correct.

question: What type of equipment is commonly used to implement an amateur radio mesh network?
answers: A 2-meter VHF transceiver with a 1,200-baud modem
A computer running EchoLink to provide interface from the radio to the internet
A wireless router running custom firmware
A 440 MHz transceiver with a 9,600-baud modem
explanation: Amateur mesh networking is commonly implemented with a commercial off-the-shelf wireless router reflashed with custom amateur firmware (such as AREDN, based on OpenWrt), which reconfigures the hardware for amateur frequencies, higher power, and wider channels than the same hardware is allowed under Part 15. A 1,200-baud 2 m or 9,600-baud 440 MHz setup is legacy AX.25 packet radio, not mesh networking, and EchoLink is VoIP-over-internet linking between individual repeaters/stations — both are real ham technologies, just not what implements a peer-to-peer wireless mesh data network.

question: Why do DX stations often transmit and receive on different frequencies?
answers: Because the DX station may be transmitting on a frequency that is prohibited to some responding stations
To separate the calling stations from the DX station
To improve operating efficiency by reducing interference
explanation: DX stations, especially rare DXpeditions, transmit on one frequency and listen on another ('split') for several genuinely simultaneous reasons: it separates the flood of calling stations from the DX station's own transmit frequency so the operator can actually hear individual callers instead of a wall of overlapping signals on top of their own; it improves operating rate/efficiency by letting the DX station work through callers faster; and it's sometimes necessary because calling stations may be restricted to band segments (e.g., an Extra-only sub-band) that don't include wherever the DX station happens to be transmitting, so calling exactly on frequency would be illegal for some would-be callers. All three reasons are true at once, so 'all of these' is correct.

question: How should you generally identify your station when attempting to contact a DX station during a contest or in a pileup?
answers: Send your full call sign once or twice
Send only the last two letters of your call sign until you make contact
Send your full call sign and grid square
Send the call sign of the DX station three times, the words “this is,” then your call sign three times
explanation: In a fast-moving pileup or contest, sending your full call sign once — or at most twice if it wasn't copied — is the efficient, expected practice: it gives the DX station exactly what's needed to identify and respond to you without wasting airtime on unnecessary repetition or on relaxed-ragchew phonetic formalities like a drawn-out 'this is... over.' Sending only partial call sign letters isn't a recognized identification practice and risks being confused with other callers, and repeatedly sending the DX station's own call sign back is also not standard pileup procedure.

question: What indicates the delay between a control operator action and the corresponding change in the transmitted signal?
explanation: Latency is the general engineering term for the delay between a triggering action and its resulting effect — in a remote-controlled or internet-linked amateur station, that's the lag between when the control operator keys up (or takes some other action) and when that action actually appears on the transmitted signal, which matters for courteous breaks in a QSO and for repeater/link timing. Jitter describes variation or inconsistency in that delay over time (not the delay itself), hang time is a repeater-specific timer that keeps the transmitter keyed briefly after input drops, and anti-VOX is a feature that prevents a station's own speaker audio from re-triggering its voice-activated transmitter — none of those describe a simple action-to-transmission delay.

question: Which of the following digital modes is designed for meteor scatter communications?
explanation: MSK144 is a WSJT-X mode purpose-built for meteor scatter: it uses short, fast transmission sequences and a minimum-shift-keying modulation tuned to exploit the very brief (fraction-of-a-second to a few-second) ionization trails left by meteors burning up in the upper atmosphere, which briefly enhance VHF propagation over paths normally out of range. WSPR is built for slow, extremely weak beacon-style propagation reporting rather than meteor pings, Hellschreiber is an old visual 'fuzzy font' mode with no meteor-scatter-specific design, and APRS is a position/data-reporting protocol unrelated to meteor scatter.

question: What information replaces signal-to-noise ratio when using the FT8 or FT4 modes in a VHF contest?
explanation: The standard FT8/FT4 QSO exchange normally includes an automatically generated signal report (a rough SNR-derived number, not a true S-meter reading), but ARRL's VHF contest rules instead require exchanging 4-character Maidenhead grid squares, since VHF/UHF contest scoring and multiplier credit is based on grid squares worked rather than signal strength — WSJT-X has a dedicated contest message format that substitutes the grid square for the usual report field. State abbreviations and serial numbers are exchange formats used in other contests (e.g., ARRL Sweepstakes, some RTTY contests), not the standard FT8/FT4 VHF contest exchange.

question: Which of the following digital modes is designed for EME communications?
explanation: Q65 (introduced in WSJT-X 2.4) was specifically developed to improve on JT65's performance on EME and other fast-fading, Doppler-spread paths typical of moonbounce, tropospheric scatter, and ionospheric scatter on VHF and higher: its decoder can average results across several consecutive receive periods to pull a decode out of signals JT65's single-period decoder would miss, and it offers multiple tone-spacing options tuned to different amounts of Doppler spread. MSK144 targets meteor scatter (much shorter, faster events), PACTOR III is an HF store-and-forward/email protocol unrelated to EME, and WSPR is a slow HF/LF/VHF beacon mode not designed around EME's specific fading behavior.

question: What technology is used for real-time tracking of balloons carrying amateur radio transmitters?
explanation: High-altitude amateur balloon payloads commonly carry a small APRS transmitter that periodically beacons GPS position, altitude, and telemetry over 2 m packet, letting trackers on the ground — and APRS-IS internet gateways — follow the flight and descent in real time on a map, using the same infrastructure as ordinary mobile/vehicle APRS tracking. FT8 and PACTOR III are HF data modes with far too slow a duty cycle for real-time position tracking, and 'bandwidth compressed LORAN' isn't a real amateur radio technology.

question: What is the characteristic of the JT65 mode?
answers: Decodes signals with a very low signal-to-noise ratio
Permits fast-scan TV transmissions over narrow bandwidth
explanation: JT65 (the predecessor to FT8, still used for EME) relies on forward error correction and long integration times (roughly a one-minute transmit cycle) to reliably decode signals well below what's audible to the ear — reportedly down around -25 dB SNR or lower in a standard reference bandwidth — which is what made it a breakthrough for weak-signal EME and HF operation. It doesn't literally use a '65 Hz bandwidth' or a '65 baud' symbol rate (the '65' names the number of possible symbol/tone values, not a literal Hz or baud figure), and it has no connection to fast-scan TV.

question: Which of the following is a method for establishing EME contacts?
answers: Judging optimum transmission times by monitoring beacons reflected from the moon
High-speed CW identification to avoid fading
explanation: Because an EME signal has a round-trip path delay to the Moon and back (roughly 2.4-2.6 seconds) plus heavy path loss and Doppler/libration fading, EME operators — on CW, SSB, or a WSJT-X digital mode alike — coordinate to transmit and receive in tightly time-synchronized alternating windows, since two stations transmitting simultaneously would waste the entire usable reflection window. Store-and-forward messaging, monitoring beacon echoes, and high-speed CW ID are all real amateur radio techniques, but none of them describes the basic method actually used to complete a two-way EME contact.

question: What digital protocol is used by APRS?
explanation: APRS is built on top of AX.25, the same connectionless packet-radio link-layer protocol used for general amateur packet networking — APRS just defines a specific set of application-layer message formats (position reports, status, messages) carried inside AX.25 frames. PACTOR and AMTOR are HF ARQ/error-correcting data protocols unrelated to APRS, and QAM is a modulation scheme, not a link-layer protocol.

question: What type of packet frame is used to transmit APRS beacon data?
explanation: APRS beacon data is transmitted as an AX.25 Unnumbered Information (UI) frame — a connectionless, unacknowledged broadcast frame type that requires no handshake or established link with any specific receiving station, which fits APRS's 'send it once, let anyone listening use it' broadcast design perfectly. Acknowledgement and Connect frames belong to AX.25's connected-mode (two-station handshaking) operation, not used for APRS beaconing, and 'Burst' isn't a real AX.25 frame type.

question: What type of modulation is used by JT65?
explanation: JT65 modulates an audio subcarrier fed into an SSB transmitter using multitone frequency-shift keying — roughly 65 discrete tones (hence the name) representing 65 possible symbol values — which is a form of multitone AFSK, not phase-shift keying, RTTY-style two-tone FSK, or QAM (which requires amplitude information in addition to phase, and isn't used by WSJT-X's weak-signal modes).

question: What does the packet path WIDE3-1 designate?
answers: Three stations are allowed on frequency, one transmitting at a time
Three subcarriers are permitted, subcarrier one is being used
Three digipeater hops are requested with one remaining
Three internet gateway stations may receive one transmission
explanation: WIDEn-N is APRS's standard generic digipeater path notation: the first number (n) is the total number of hops originally requested when the path was set, and the second number (N) counts down as each digipeater along the way relays the packet and decrements it. WIDE3-1 means the path started as WIDE3-3 (three hops requested), has already been relayed twice, and one hop remains before the packet should stop being repeated further.

question: How do APRS stations relay data?
explanation: APRS stations relay data through packet digipeaters — stations (often on hilltops or towers) configured to automatically receive and retransmit APRS packets addressed to a generic path alias like WIDE1-1 or WIDE2-2, extending the effective range of low-power mobile and portable stations far beyond simplex range. The other choices describe unrelated technologies: ACK/NAK relay is a connected-mode packet concept, and C4FM/DMR are digital voice repeater systems, not how APRS actually propagates its packets.

question: Which of the following types of modulation is used for data emissions below 30 MHz?
answers: DTMF tones modulating an FM signal
explanation: Below 30 MHz, essentially all amateur data/digital modes (RTTY, PSK31, most WSJT-X modes, PACTOR, etc.) are transmitted as frequency-shift-keyed subcarriers — either the carrier itself is shifted directly, or an audio tone fed into an SSB transmitter produces the equivalent effect. DTMF-on-FM is a control-tone signaling technique, not a general HF data mode, and pulse modulation and spread spectrum, while legal for amateur use, are almost exclusively used on VHF/UHF/microwave, not for routine HF data emissions.

question: Which of the following synchronizes WSJT-X digital mode transmit/receive timing?
explanation: WSJT-X's fixed, precisely timed transmit/receive sequences (e.g., FT8's 15-second cycles starting exactly on UTC :00, :15, :30, :45) only work if every station's computer clock is synchronized to within about a second of UTC, typically via NTP — the software uses wall-clock time itself, not any signal embedded in the received audio, to decide when to start decoding and when to transmit. That's why accurate computer clock synchronization (not tone-frequency alignment or an embedded sync field/pulse in the RF) is the actual mechanism, and a drifted PC clock is a very common cause of a new digital-mode operator failing to decode or be decoded.

question: To what does the "4" in FT4 refer?
answers: Multiples of 4 bits of user information
explanation: FT4 uses 4-GFSK — four-tone, continuous-phase Gaussian frequency-shift keying — as its modulation, and that four-tone scheme is where the '4' in the mode's name comes from; it's a faster, contest-oriented sibling of FT8 built on the same basic MFSK approach with different tone count and timing. It isn't a reference to multiples of bits per symbol or to transmit/receive cycles per minute (FT4's cycle is actually about 7.5 seconds, giving roughly 8 cycles/minute, not 4) — the '4' specifically names the modulation's tone count.

question: Which of the following is characteristic of the FST4 mode?
explanation: FST4 modulates using 4-tone Gaussian FSK (matching its name), supports a range of selectable transmit/receive sequence lengths from 15 seconds up through 1800 seconds (30 minutes) depending on band conditions and how weak a signal needs to be recovered, and correspondingly offers seven different tone spacings tuned to those different sequence lengths. All three of these are genuinely true characteristics of FST4 at once, so 'all of these' is correct — the mode (and its beacon-style variant FST4W) targets LF/MF and weak-signal HF work where very long integration times pay off.

question: Which of these digital modes does not support keyboard-to-keyboard operation?
explanation: WSPR (Weak Signal Propagation Reporter) transmits a fixed, compressed message automatically generated by the software — callsign, 4-character grid square, and power level — making it a beacon/propagation-reporting mode, not a means for a free-text back-and-forth conversation, so it doesn't support keyboard-to-keyboard chat. RTTY, PSK31, and MFSK16 all do support real-time free-form typed conversation between operators, which is the distinguishing feature the question is testing.

question: What is the length of an FT8 transmission cycle?
answers: It varies with the amount of data
explanation: An FT8 transmission cycle is 15 seconds long, with transmissions starting precisely on UTC second boundaries that are multiples of 15 (e.g., :00, :15, :30, :45) — a fixed, non-negotiable length that lets every station in a QSO stay synchronized purely off computer clock time. It's not 8 seconds (that's just the numeral in the mode's name, unrelated to the timing), not 30 seconds (that's closer to a JT65 cycle), and it doesn't vary with data content the way a free-running mode might.

question: How does Q65 differ from JT65?
explanation: Q65's key improvement over JT65 is that its decoder can combine (average) information across several consecutive receive periods to extract a decode from a signal affected by fast fading and Doppler spread — common on EME, tropospheric scatter, and ionospheric scatter paths — something JT65's single-period decoder can't do, and it's what makes Q65 noticeably better than JT65 on those specific difficult paths. Q65 doesn't add keyboard-to-keyboard support (neither mode has it) and doesn't use literal quadrature/QAM modulation (both remain multi-tone FSK-family modes), so the other choices misdescribe the actual difference.

question: Which of the following HF digital modes can be used to transfer binary files?
explanation: PACTOR (used heavily for Winlink email-over-radio) is a robust ARQ (automatic repeat request) data protocol designed to reliably carry arbitrary binary data — including compressed email with attachments — using error detection and automatic retransmission of corrupted blocks, not just printable text. PSK31, RTTY, and AMTOR are all fundamentally character/text-oriented transmission modes not designed for general-purpose binary file transfer.

question: Which of the following HF digital modes uses variable-length character coding?
explanation: PSK31 uses 'Varicode,' a Morse-like scheme in which more common characters get shorter bit patterns and less common characters get longer ones, minimizing average transmission time for typical English text — conceptually the same idea as Morse code assigning 'E' a single dit. RTTY (fixed 5-bit Baudot), PACTOR (fixed-length coded ARQ blocks), and MT63 (fixed-width multi-tone symbols) all use fixed-length coding schemes instead, which is what distinguishes PSK31 here.

question: Which of these digital modes has the narrowest bandwidth?
explanation: FT8's eight-tone FSK signal occupies roughly 50 Hz of bandwidth, narrower than 170 Hz-shift/45-baud RTTY (on the order of 250-300 Hz once sidebands are counted), MFSK16 (about 316 Hz across its 16 tones), or PACTOR IV (which can use up to 2.4 kHz in its higher-speed modes) — so among these four choices, FT8 is by far the narrowest, a direct consequence of its design priority (extreme weak-signal sensitivity) over speed.

question: What is the difference between direct FSK and audio FSK?
answers: Direct FSK modulates the transmitter VFO
Direct FSK can transmit higher baud rates
explanation: 'Direct FSK' (sometimes called hardware FSK) shifts the transmitter's actual RF oscillator/VFO frequency directly between mark and space with no audio tones involved, while 'audio FSK' (AFSK) generates the two tones as an audio signal fed into a conventional SSB transmitter, which up-converts them to RF as a byproduct of ordinary SSB modulation. Neither approach is inherently narrower in bandwidth or capable of higher baud rates purely because it's direct versus audio — the real difference is in the modulation path and hardware used, which is why 'modulates the transmitter VFO' (not bandwidth or speed) is the correct, specific distinguishing fact.

question: How do ALE stations establish contact?
answers: ALE constantly scans a list of frequencies, activating the radio when the designated call sign is received
ALE radios monitor an internet site for the frequency they are being paged on
ALE radios send a constant tone code to establish a frequency for future use
ALE radios activate when they hear their signal echoed by back scatter
explanation: Automatic Link Establishment (ALE) radios continuously and automatically scan a preprogrammed list of channels/frequencies in the background; when another ALE station transmits a call containing your station's address on one of those channels, your radio recognizes it, stops scanning, and automatically establishes the link on the best available channel — all without an operator manually tuning around. This automated call-and-scan process is what 'automatic' actually refers to in ALE, and it's widely used for MARS, emergency, and HF traffic networks. It doesn't depend on an internet paging site, a reserved constant tone-code channel, or backscatter echo detection, which are all incorrect mechanisms offered as distractors.

question: Which of these digital modes has the highest data throughput under clear communication conditions?
explanation: PACTOR IV can achieve throughput up to roughly 5,512 bps of real (uncompressed) data, and higher effective rates with text compression enabled — far faster under clear conditions than FT8 (deliberately slow, since it trades speed for the ability to decode signals far below the noise floor), or than standard RTTY/MFSK16 configurations (both well under 100 bps effective). That's exactly why PACTOR IV is the mode of choice for Winlink email-over-radio whenever propagation is good enough to support it, making it the correct answer for highest data throughput under clear communication conditions among these four choices.

question: What is the approximate maximum separation measured along the surface of the Earth between two stations communicating by EME?
answers: 2,000 miles, if the moon is at perigee
2,000 miles, if the moon is at apogee
5,000 miles, if the moon is at perigee
12,000 miles, if the moon is “visible” by both stations
explanation: The maximum ground separation for an EME (moonbounce) contact is set by geometry, not by lunar distance: both stations need the Moon above their local horizon at the same instant, and the farthest apart two such stations can be is when the Moon sits right on the horizon for each of them simultaneously, which works out to roughly 12,000 miles along the Earth's surface (a bit under half of Earth's circumference). Perigee and apogee change the Earth-Moon distance and therefore the path loss of the echo, but they don't change this horizon-visibility limit, which is why the correct answer ties the 12,000-mile figure to mutual visibility of the Moon rather than to perigee or apogee.

question: What characterizes libration fading of an EME signal?
answers: A slow change in the pitch of the CW signal
A gradual loss of signal as the sun rises
The returning echo is several hertz lower in frequency than the transmitted signal
explanation: Libration fading is the fast, ragged, irregular fading characteristic of EME signals, caused by the Moon's libration (its slow wobble/rotation relative to Earth), which constantly shifts the relative positions of the many rough reflecting facets on the lunar surface and produces multipath that beats against itself unpredictably. It is not a smooth pitch change, a sunrise-related fade, or a fixed frequency offset of the echo (a Doppler shift can occur, but that's a separate effect from libration fading and isn't several hertz lower by definition).

question: When scheduling EME contacts, which of these conditions will generally result in the least path loss?
answers: When the Moon is at perigee
When the Moon is at apogee
When the MUF is above 30 MHz
explanation: Path loss in EME is dominated by the total round-trip distance the signal travels (free-space spreading loss over roughly half a million miles), so the least loss occurs when the Moon is at perigee, its closest approach to Earth. Whether the Moon is full has no bearing on its RF reflectivity, and apogee is the far end of the orbit (more loss, the opposite of perigee); MUF is an HF ionospheric-refraction concept and is irrelevant to VHF/UHF EME paths, which pass through the ionosphere rather than being refracted by it.

question: In what direction does an electromagnetic wave travel?
answers: It depends on the phase angle of the magnetic field
It travels parallel to the electric and magnetic fields
It depends on the phase angle of the electric field
It travels at a right angle to the electric and magnetic fields
explanation: An electromagnetic wave propagates along the direction given by the Poynting vector, E x H, which by definition is at a right angle to both the electric (E) and magnetic (H) field vectors. The other choices misdescribe this relationship: the wave doesn't travel parallel to the fields, and its direction isn't a function of either field's phase angle -- the fields' phase relationship affects wave impedance and polarization behavior, not propagation direction.

question: How are the component fields of an electromagnetic wave oriented?
answers: They are 90 degrees out of phase
explanation: In a plane electromagnetic wave, the electric and magnetic field vectors are oriented at right angles to each other (and both are perpendicular to the direction of travel), forming the classic mutually-orthogonal E-H-direction triad. They are not parallel or merely tangential to one another, and while 90 degrees is the right number, that distractor describes a time-phase relationship, not the spatial orientation the question is asking about -- in free space the E and H fields are actually in time-phase with each other, just spatially orthogonal.

question: What should be done to continue a long-distance contact when the MUF for that path decreases due to darkness?
answers: Switch to a higher frequency HF band
Switch to a lower frequency HF band
Change to an antenna with a higher takeoff angle
Change to an antenna with greater beam width
explanation: As darkness reduces solar ionization of the F layer, the Maximum Usable Frequency for a given path drops; to keep a contact going you have to move down to a lower HF band that is now below the reduced MUF so the ionosphere can still refract the signal back to Earth. Moving to a higher band only makes the problem worse (the signal will punch through the weaker ionosphere instead of refracting), and changing antenna takeoff angle or beamwidth doesn't compensate for operating above the MUF.

question: Atmospheric ducts capable of propagating microwave signals often form over what geographic feature?
explanation: Tropospheric ducts capable of carrying microwave signals form most readily over large bodies of water, where a stable, moist, cooler air layer near the surface sits under warmer air aloft, creating the temperature/humidity inversion and refractive-index gradient needed to trap and duct the signal along the surface for extended distances. Mountain ranges and generic cloud types (stratocumulus, nimbus) are not the classic mechanism the pool associates with tropo ducting.

question: When a meteor strikes the Earth’s atmosphere, a linear ionized region is formed at what region of the ionosphere?
explanation: A meteor entering the atmosphere burns up and ionizes a narrow, linear column of air in the E region (roughly 70-100 km altitude) -- the same altitude band associated with sporadic-E -- and that short-lived ionized trail is what briefly reflects VHF signals for meteor-scatter contacts. It's not the F1 or F2 regions (higher altitude, driven by daytime solar UV) nor the D region (lower, mainly an absorption layer rather than a reflecting one).

question: Which of the following frequency ranges is most suited for meteor-scatter communications?
explanation: Meteor-scatter work is best suited to roughly 28 MHz - 148 MHz (essentially 10 meters through 2 meters), the range where meteor trails are dense enough to give a useful, if brief, reflection and where the signal isn't already reliably propagating by normal ionospheric skip. Lower HF frequencies (1.8-14 MHz) don't need meteor scatter because F-layer skip already covers them, and frequencies above about 148-220 MHz are generally too high for the short-lived, less-efficient meteor trails to reflect well.

question: What determines the speed of electromagnetic waves through a medium?
explanation: The speed at which an electromagnetic wave moves through a medium is set by that medium's index of refraction, n, via v = c/n -- a higher index slows the wave down relative to its free-space (vacuum) speed c. Resistance and reactance describe lumped circuit elements, not wave propagation through a medium; birefringence describes a material splitting a wave into two different-speed polarization components (a related but distinct phenomenon); evanescence describes a non-propagating, exponentially decaying near-field wave, not propagation speed.

question: What is a typical range for tropospheric duct propagation of microwave signals?
explanation: Tropospheric ducting of microwave signals typically carries signals on the order of 100 to 300 miles, well beyond simple line-of-sight but far short of ionospheric-skip distances. Ten to fifty miles is really just ordinary VHF/UHF line-of-sight range, while 1,200 or 2,500 miles are far beyond what a single tropospheric duct achieves (those distances belong to ionospheric propagation mechanisms instead).

question: What is most likely to result in auroral propagation?
answers: Extreme low-pressure areas in polar regions
explanation: Auroral propagation results from severe geomagnetic storms, which inject energetic charged particles into the polar upper atmosphere; those particles ionize and roughen the E-region there, letting VHF signals scatter off the disturbed region. Quiet geomagnetic conditions are the opposite of what's needed, meteor showers cause meteor-scatter (a different mechanism entirely), and low-pressure weather systems are a tropospheric phenomenon unrelated to auroral/ionospheric activity.

question: Which of these emission modes is best for auroral propagation?
explanation: CW is the preferred mode for auroral propagation because the auroral E-region reflection introduces heavy, rapid Doppler spreading that smears and distorts a signal into a rasping, fluttery buzz -- voice modes (SSB, FM) become unintelligible and RTTY's narrow mark/space tones and timing get corrupted, but a simple on/off-keyed CW tone, even badly distorted, can usually still be copied by ear.

question: What are circularly polarized electromagnetic waves?
answers: Waves with an electric field bent into a circular shape
Waves with rotating electric and magnetic fields
Waves produced by a loop antenna
explanation: A circularly polarized wave is one whose electric and magnetic field vectors rotate around the direction of propagation as the wave travels, tracing a circular (rather than fixed-plane) pattern -- this is a real, physical rotation of the field orientation over time, not a field literally bent into a circle, not a wave that circles the globe, and not simply defined by the type of antenna (a loop) that might produce it.

question: Where is transequatorial propagation (TEP) most likely to occur?
answers: Between points separated by 2,000 miles to 3,000 miles over a path perpendicular to the geomagnetic equator
Between points located 1,500 miles to 2,000 miles apart on the geomagnetic equator
Between points located at each other’s antipode
Through the region where the terminator crosses the geographic equator
explanation: Transequatorial propagation (TEP) is most likely between points 2,000-3,000 miles apart along a path that crosses roughly perpendicular to the geomagnetic equator, because it exploits the pair of F-region ionization crests (the equatorial anomaly) that straddle the magnetic equator, letting a signal hop between the two enhanced regions. It is not a path running along the magnetic equator itself, not antipodal points, and it isn't defined by where the day/night terminator crosses the geographic equator (that's a separate, grayline-related idea).

question: What is the approximate maximum range for signals using transequatorial propagation?
explanation: Under favorable conditions, transequatorial propagation can extend out to roughly 5,000 miles, well beyond the more typical 2,000-3,000-mile TEP range, when the equatorial ionization anomaly is strongly developed. The other listed distances either undershoot (1,000 or 2,500 miles) or overshoot (7,500 miles) the figure given in the current question pool for maximum TEP range.

question: At what time of day is transequatorial propagation most likely to occur?
explanation: TEP is most likely in the afternoon or early evening (roughly around local sunset along the path), which is when the equatorial ionization anomaly's two F-region crests are most strongly developed for the day. Morning and midday haven't built up the necessary ionization enhancement yet, and by late night the anomaly has largely decayed.

question: What are “extraordinary” and “ordinary” waves?
answers: Extraordinary waves exhibit rare long-skip propagation, compared to ordinary waves, which travel shorter distances
Independently propagating, elliptically polarized waves created in the ionosphere
explanation: 'Extraordinary' and 'ordinary' waves refer to the two independently propagating, elliptically polarized wave components that a radio signal splits into when it enters the ionosphere, a result of the magneto-ionic (Earth's-magnetic-field) splitting of the wave -- each component has a slightly different refractive index and absorption behavior. This isn't about rare versus common skip distances, long-path versus short-path routes, or a simple refracted-ray-versus-reflected-wave distinction.

question: Which of the following paths is most likely to support long-distance propagation on 160 meters?
explanation: Long-distance 160-meter propagation favors a path that lies entirely in darkness, because 160m suffers heavy D-layer absorption in daylight; with no solar ionization of the D layer at night, that absorption largely disappears and the F-layer refraction that does the actual long-haul work can operate with far less loss. A sunlit path suffers the opposite problem, and high latitude or strict north-south orientation aren't themselves the controlling factor -- darkness along the path is.

question: On which of the following amateur bands is long-path propagation most frequent?
explanation: Long-path propagation shows up most often on 40 and 20 meters, bands where the F layer reliably supports full round-the-world skip and where the long-path direction (often through darkness or grayline while the short path sits in daylight, or vice versa) can actually have lower loss than the short path. 160/80 meters are usually too absorbed for that kind of long-haul skip, and the VHF pairs (10/6 meters, 6/2 meters) generally lack the sustained F-layer refraction needed for true long-path openings.

question: What effect does lowering a signal’s transmitted elevation angle have on ionospheric HF skip propagation?
answers: The distance covered by each hop increases
explanation: Lowering a signal's transmitted elevation (takeoff) angle sends it out toward the ionosphere at a shallower angle, which increases the ground distance covered before it refracts back down -- i.e., it lengthens each hop. It does not decrease the MUF for that path; by the secant law, a lower elevation angle actually raises the usable oblique-incidence MUF (more distractor than fact), and Faraday rotation and critical frequency aren't governed by transmit elevation angle at all.

question: How does the maximum range of ground-wave propagation change when the signal frequency is increased?
explanation: Ground-wave range shrinks as frequency goes up, because the ground itself is a lossy conductor and the induced surface currents that carry a ground wave suffer greater attenuation per wavelength at higher frequencies. This is exactly why AM broadcast stations near 1 MHz get useful ground-wave range while VHF ground wave barely reaches beyond line of sight; there's no 8 MHz 'peak,' and range doesn't stay the same or increase with frequency.

question: At what time of year is sporadic-E propagation most likely to occur?
answers: Around the solstices, especially the summer solstice
Around the solstices, especially the winter solstice
Around the equinoxes, especially the spring equinox
Around the equinoxes, especially the fall equinox
explanation: Sporadic-E propagation peaks around the solstices, and most strongly around the summer solstice, tied to seasonal wind-shear and tidal mechanisms that concentrate metallic ion layers in the E region during Northern Hemisphere summer. It is not primarily an equinox phenomenon (that secondary bump is much smaller), and it favors the summer solstice over the winter one.

question: What is the effect of chordal-hop propagation?
answers: The signal experiences less loss compared to multi-hop propagation, which uses Earth as a reflector
The MUF for chordal-hop propagation is much lower than for normal skip propagation
Atmospheric noise is reduced in the direction of chordal-hop propagation
Signals travel faster along ionospheric chords
explanation: Chordal-hop propagation refracts a signal from one ionospheric region to another without an intervening bounce off the (lossy) ground, so it experiences noticeably less loss than ordinary multi-hop skip, which loses energy at every ground reflection. It doesn't lower the MUF, it doesn't reduce atmospheric noise in that direction, and signals don't travel faster along ionospheric chords -- the benefit is purely reduced attenuation from skipping the ground bounce.

question: At what time of day is sporadic-E propagation most likely to occur?
explanation: Sporadic-E is most likely to occur between sunrise and sunset -- i.e., during daylight hours -- consistent with the diurnal wind-shear/ion-layer concentration mechanism that builds up the sporadic-E patches; nighttime Es does happen but is considerably less common than the daytime peak.

question: What is chordal-hop propagation?
answers: Propagation away from the great circle bearing between stations
Successive ionospheric refractions without an intermediate reflection from the ground
Signals reflected back toward the transmitting station
explanation: Chordal-hop propagation is defined as successive ionospheric refractions occurring without an intermediate reflection off the ground between them -- the signal bounces from one ionospheric refraction point to the next directly. It is not propagation that departs from the great-circle bearing, not a mechanism tied to crossing the geomagnetic equator (that's transequatorial propagation), and not signals reflecting back toward the transmitter (that would be a backscatter effect).

question: What type of polarization is supported by ground-wave propagation?
explanation: Ground-wave propagation supports vertical polarization. A horizontally polarized wave traveling along the surface has its electric field effectively short-circuited by the conducting ground (the induced image currents cancel the field at the surface), causing rapid attenuation, while a vertically polarized wave's field is oriented perpendicular to the ground and couples efficiently into surface currents, letting it travel much farther -- especially over highly conductive salt water. This is exactly why AM broadcast and marine MF stations use vertical antennas.

question: What is the cause of short-term radio blackouts?
explanation: Short-term (sudden) HF radio blackouts are caused by solar flares: a flare's burst of X-rays reaches Earth in about 8 minutes and sharply increases D-layer ionization on the sunlit side, producing a Sudden Ionospheric Disturbance that raises HF absorption to the point of a blackout lasting minutes to roughly an hour. Coronal mass ejections instead drive geomagnetic storms with effects that arrive a day or more later and last longer; sunspots by themselves aren't the direct cause, and a north-oriented interplanetary magnetic field is associated with quieter, not disturbed, conditions.

question: What is indicated by a rising A-index or K-index?
answers: Increasing disturbance of the geomagnetic field
Decreasing disturbance of the geomagnetic field
Higher levels of solar UV radiation
An increase in the critical frequency
explanation: A rising A-index or K-index indicates increasing disturbance of the geomagnetic field -- these are standard geomagnetic activity indices (K measured over 3-hour intervals, A as a derived daily average) computed from magnetometer data, and higher values mean a more disturbed magnetosphere, generally correlating with worse HF conditions from increased absorption. They are not measures of solar UV output or of the ionosphere's critical frequency, which are tracked by separate parameters.

question: Which of the following signal paths is most likely to experience high levels of absorption when the A-index or K-index is elevated?
explanation: When the A-index or K-index is elevated, the auroral oval is the path most likely to suffer high absorption, since geomagnetic storms dump energetic particles into the polar regions, enhancing D/E-region ionization and absorption right where the auroral oval sits. Transequatorial, sporadic-E, and NVIS (near-vertical incidence skywave) paths aren't primarily polar routes, so they are far less directly affected by a rise in geomagnetic disturbance indices.

question: What does the value of Bz (B sub z) represent?
answers: North-south strength of the interplanetary magnetic field
explanation: Bz is the north-south component of the interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) carried outward from the Sun by the solar wind -- a specific, defined space-weather parameter, distinct from concepts like geomagnetic field 'stability' in general, ionospheric critical frequency, or the duration of long-delayed echoes.

question: What orientation of Bz (B sub z) increases the likelihood that charged particles from the Sun will cause disturbed conditions?
explanation: A southward-pointing Bz increases the likelihood of disturbed geomagnetic conditions, because it opposes Earth's own northward-pointing field at the dayside magnetopause, allowing magnetic reconnection that lets solar wind energy and particles couple efficiently into the magnetosphere and drive storms/substorms. A northward Bz tends to shield the magnetosphere and is associated with quieter conditions, and eastward/westward orientations are far less geoeffective than a southward one.

question: How does the VHF/UHF radio horizon compare to the geographic horizon?
explanation: The VHF/UHF radio horizon extends roughly 15 percent farther than the plain geographic (optical/line-of-sight) horizon, because the troposphere's normal refractive-index gradient bends radio waves slightly downward, effectively curving them around the Earth a bit -- often modeled using an 'effective Earth radius' about 4/3 of the true radius, which works out to about that 15 percent extension. It is not 20 percent nearer, 50 percent farther, or essentially the same as the geographic horizon.

question: Which of the following indicates the greatest solar flare intensity?
explanation: Solar flares are classified by X-ray intensity into letter classes A, B, C, M, and X, each roughly ten times more intense than the one before, with X-class flares being the most intense category (and themselves further subdivided, e.g., X1, X10, with no fixed upper limit). 'Class Z' is not a real flare classification, and A and M are lower on the scale than X.

question: Which of the following is the space-weather term for an extreme geomagnetic storm?
explanation: NOAA's space-weather G-scale for geomagnetic storms runs from G1 (minor) to G5 (extreme), so G5 is the designation for the most severe (extreme) geomagnetic storm category. The other choices (B9, M9, X5) belong to the unrelated solar-flare X-ray classification scale, not the geomagnetic-storm G-scale.

question: What type of data is reported by amateur radio propagation reporting networks?
explanation: Amateur radio propagation reporting networks -- systems like the Reverse Beacon Network, PSK Reporter, and WSPRnet -- report actual received digital-mode and CW signal spots (call sign, frequency, time, and signal strength/SNR) gathered automatically by monitoring stations worldwide. They don't report raw geophysical measurements like solar flux, electric field intensity, or magnetic declination; those come from dedicated space-weather and geomagnetic observatories, not ham propagation-reporting networks.

question: What does the 304A solar parameter measure?
answers: The ratio of X-ray flux to radio flux, correlated to sunspot number
UV emissions at 304 angstroms, correlated to the solar flux index
The solar wind velocity at an angle of 304 degrees from the solar equator, correlated to geomagnetic storms
The solar emission at 304 GHz, correlated to X-ray flare levels
explanation: The 304A parameter measures solar ultraviolet emission at a wavelength of 304 angstroms (from ionized helium high in the Sun's atmosphere), and it correlates well with the solar flux index (SFI) and with F-region ionization levels, making it a same-day proxy for daytime HF propagation conditions. It is not an X-ray-to-radio-flux ratio, not a solar-wind-angle parameter, and not a GHz-band emission tied to flare classification.

question: What does VOACAP software model?
explanation: VOACAP (Voice of America Coverage Analysis Program) is HF propagation prediction software: given transmitter power, antenna patterns, time of day/season, and solar activity inputs, it models expected signal strength and reliability on point-to-point or area-coverage HF paths via the ionosphere. It has nothing to do with AC circuit voltage/current/impedance calculations, and it models HF (not VHF) skywave propagation.

question: Which of the following is indicated by a sudden rise in radio background noise across a large portion of the HF spectrum?
answers: A coronal mass ejection impact or a solar flare has occurred
Transequatorial propagation on 6 meters is likely
Long-path propagation on the higher HF bands is likely
explanation: A sudden, broad rise in HF background noise typically signals that a coronal mass ejection has struck the magnetosphere or that a solar flare has occurred, since the resulting geomagnetic disturbance and particle precipitation raise the ionospheric/atmospheric noise floor across a wide swath of the HF spectrum. A tropospheric temperature inversion is a weather phenomenon tied to VHF/UHF ducting, not broadband HF noise, and a noise-floor spike by itself doesn't indicate that transequatorial or long-path propagation is likely.

question: Which of the following limits the highest frequency signal that can be accurately displayed on a digital oscilloscope?
answers: Sampling rate of the analog-to-digital converter
explanation: On a digital storage scope, the ADC samples the input at a fixed rate; per the Nyquist criterion you need noticeably more than two samples per cycle to faithfully reconstruct a waveform, so the ADC's sampling rate sets the practical ceiling on the highest frequency that can be accurately displayed (correct answer A). The ADC's reference voltage sets amplitude range, not frequency response, and "Q of the circuit" is a resonant-circuit concept that has nothing to do with a scope's display bandwidth, so B and C are wrong and D ("all of these") is therefore wrong too.

question: Which of the following parameters does a spectrum analyzer display on the vertical and horizontal axes?
explanation: A spectrum analyzer sweeps across a range of frequencies (horizontal axis) and plots the amplitude of whatever signal energy it finds at each frequency (vertical axis) - this is its defining feature, contrasted with an oscilloscope which plots amplitude vs. time. SWR isn't something a plain spectrum analyzer measures on its own (that requires a directional bridge/coupler and, for full sweep, a tracking generator/VNA), which rules out the SWR-based choices C and D, leaving B (amplitude and frequency) correct.

question: Which of the following test instruments is used to display spurious signals and/or intermodulation distortion products generated by an SSB transmitter?
explanation: A spectrum analyzer displays signal amplitude across a span of frequencies, so an SSB transmitter's wanted output plus any spurious emissions or intermodulation distortion products appear as separate, measurable peaks alongside the carrier - exactly the tool for this job (B). A logic analyzer captures digital logic-level timing, not RF spectral content; a "differential resolver" isn't a standard piece of RF test gear; and a network analyzer characterizes a device's response (gain, return loss) to a known stimulus rather than displaying the free spurious content actually radiated by a transmitter, so A, C, and D are wrong.

question: How is compensation of an oscilloscope probe performed?
answers: A square wave is displayed, and the probe is adjusted until the horizontal portions of the displayed wave are as nearly flat as possible
A high frequency sine wave is displayed, and the probe is adjusted for maximum amplitude
A frequency standard is displayed, and the probe is adjusted until the deflection time is accurate
A DC voltage standard is displayed, and the probe is adjusted until the displayed voltage is accurate
explanation: Standard probe compensation procedure: connect the probe to the scope's built-in square-wave calibration output, then adjust the small trimmer capacitor in the probe body (or its connector) until the horizontal top and bottom of the displayed square wave are as flat as possible - overshoot ("peaking") on the corners means overcompensation, and a rounded/tilted top means undercompensation (correct answer A). The other choices describe compensating for entirely different things (deflection timing, DC accuracy, or a sine wave's amplitude) that aren't how probe compensation is actually done.

question: What is the purpose of using a prescaler with a frequency counter?
answers: Amplify low-level signals for more accurate counting
Multiply a higher frequency signal so a low-frequency counter can display the operating frequency
Prevent oscillation in a low-frequency counter circuit
Reduce the signal frequency to within the counter's operating range
explanation: A prescaler is a fixed-ratio digital divider (e.g. ÷10 or ÷100) placed ahead of a frequency counter's own counting circuitry, so a signal whose frequency is higher than the counter can natively handle gets divided down into the counter's working range before being counted; the counter (or the operator) then multiplies the displayed result back up by the known division ratio to show the true input frequency (correct answer D - "reduce the signal frequency to within the counter's operating range"). Answer B describes the opposite operation (multiplying, not dividing) and is a common wrong-answer trap; A and C describe unrelated functions (amplification and oscillation suppression) that a prescaler doesn't perform.

question: What is the effect of aliasing on a digital oscilloscope when displaying a waveform?
answers: A false, jittery low-frequency version of the waveform is displayed
The waveform DC offset will be inaccurate
Calibration of the vertical scale is no longer valid
Excessive blanking occurs, which prevents display of the waveform
explanation: Aliasing occurs on a digital scope when the sampling rate is too low relative to the input frequency (violating the Nyquist criterion of at least ~2x the highest frequency component), so the ADC's sparse samples land at a different phase on each cycle and get reconstructed by the scope into a false waveform that appears at a much lower frequency than the real signal, and that false image jitters/drifts because the phase relationship between the sampling clock and the real signal keeps changing (correct answer A). It's a reconstruction artifact, not a DC-offset, vertical-calibration, or blanking problem, which rules out B, C, and D.

question: Which of the following is an advantage of using an antenna analyzer compared to an SWR bridge?
answers: Antenna analyzers automatically tune your antenna for resonance
Antenna analyzers compute SWR and impedance automatically
Antenna analyzers display a time-varying representation of the modulation envelope
explanation: An antenna analyzer contains its own low-power RF source, a built-in bridge, and enough processing to directly compute and display both SWR and complex impedance (R + jX) at the frequency you dial in, without needing a separate transmitter, external SWR meter, or manual calculation - a plain SWR bridge only gives you raw forward/reflected readings that you (or an attached transmitter and meter) have to interpret (correct answer B). Antenna analyzers do not automatically retune/adjust your antenna for you (that overstates what they do, ruling out A), and displaying a modulation envelope over time is an oscilloscope/spectrum-analyzer function unrelated to antenna analysis (ruling out C), so D ("all of these") is wrong because A and C are false.

question: Which of the following is used to measure SWR?
explanation: SWR can legitimately be derived or displayed by a directional wattmeter (from its forward/reflected power readings), by a vector network analyzer (from the magnitude of its S11 reflection coefficient), and by a dedicated antenna analyzer (from its own built-in bridge) - all three are valid, commonly used ways hams measure SWR, so "all of these choices are correct" (D) is the right answer.

question: Which of the following is good practice when using an oscilloscope probe?
answers: Minimize the length of the probe's ground connection
Never use a high-impedance probe to measure a low-impedance circuit
Never use a DC-coupled probe to measure an AC circuit
explanation: Keeping an oscilloscope probe's ground (return) lead as short as possible minimizes the series inductance in the ground path, which otherwise resonates with the probe's and circuit's stray capacitance and rings/distorts fast edges - this is standard good practice, especially for higher-frequency or fast-transient measurements (correct answer A). B and C are absolute "never" statements that are simply untrue in general: a high-impedance probe can still be used on a low-impedance circuit if you only care about voltage (its loading effect is just less of a concern there), and a DC-coupled probe reads AC content just fine (the AC rides on whatever DC baseline is present) - so D ("all of these") is wrong because B and C don't hold.

question: Which trigger mode is most effective when using an oscilloscope to measure a linear power supply’s output ripple?
explanation: A linear (non-switching) power supply's output ripple is directly derived from, and synchronized to, the AC mains waveform (60 Hz for half-wave rectification, 120 Hz for full-wave) - triggering the scope from its internal "Line" trigger (tapped directly from the AC power feeding the scope) locks the display to that same mains reference, giving a rock-stable view of the ripple even if the ripple signal itself is small or noisy (correct answer D). Edge or level triggering directly off the low-amplitude ripple can be unreliable, and single-shot triggering is meant for one-time transient captures, not a continuously repeating waveform like power-supply ripple.

question: Which of the following can be measured with an antenna analyzer?
answers: Resonant frequency of a tuned circuit
explanation: Modern swept-frequency antenna analyzers do far more than a simple SWR bridge: by sweeping frequency and tracking the reflection/impedance response, many models can compute a feedline's velocity factor and physical length (essentially a frequency-domain reflectometry technique, similar in principle to TDR), and by sweeping through a tuned circuit and finding where reactance crosses zero, they can find that circuit's resonant frequency - all three listed measurements are genuine capabilities of common antenna analyzers, so D ("all of these") is correct.

question: Which of the following factors most affects the accuracy of a frequency counter?
explanation: A frequency counter works by comparing the unknown input signal against its own internal time base (reference) oscillator over a precise gate interval; any percentage error in that time base translates directly and proportionally into the same percentage error in the displayed frequency reading, which is why time base accuracy is overwhelmingly the dominant factor in a counter's overall accuracy (correct answer B). Input attenuator accuracy affects how well the counter handles signal amplitude (not the count itself), decade dividers divide by exact integer ratios with no error contribution, and logic temperature coefficient is a comparatively minor second-order effect.

question: What is the significance of voltmeter sensitivity expressed in ohms per volt?
answers: The full scale reading of the voltmeter multiplied by its ohms per volt rating is the input impedance of the voltmeter
The reading in volts multiplied by the ohms per volt rating will determine the power drawn by the device under test
The reading in ohms divided by the ohms per volt rating will determine the voltage applied to the circuit
The full scale reading in amps divided by ohms per volt rating will determine the size of shunt needed
explanation: A voltmeter's sensitivity, rated in ohms-per-volt, tells you the meter's internal (movement) resistance per volt of full-scale range; multiplying that ohms-per-volt figure by the full-scale voltage of whichever range is selected gives the voltmeter's actual input impedance on that range (correct answer A) - a critical number because a low-impedance meter can noticeably load down (and give a falsely low reading on) a high-impedance circuit under test. The other choices misapply the units to power, applied voltage, or shunt sizing in ways that don't correspond to what ohms-per-volt actually measures.

question: Which S parameter is equivalent to forward gain?
explanation: In two-port S-parameter notation, S21 is the ratio of the signal coming out of port 2 to the signal going into port 1 - i.e., forward transmission, which is exactly forward gain (correct answer C). S11 and S22 are reflection coefficients (return loss/VSWR) at ports 1 and 2 respectively, and S12 is reverse transmission (isolation), so none of A, B, or D describe forward gain.

question: Which S parameter represents input port return loss or reflection coefficient (equivalent to VSWR)?
explanation: S11 is the ratio of the reflected signal at port 1 to the signal incident on port 1 with all other ports terminated - that's precisely the reflection coefficient at the input port, which corresponds directly to input return loss and VSWR (correct answer A). S22 is the same concept but at the output port, while S21 and S12 are transmission (gain/isolation) parameters, not reflection parameters, so B, C, and D are wrong.

question: What three test loads are used to calibrate an RF vector network analyzer?
answers: Short circuit, open circuit, and 50 ohms
Short circuit, open circuit, and resonant circuit
50 ohms through 1/8 wavelength, 1/4 wavelength, and 1/2 wavelength of coaxial cable
explanation: A vector network analyzer is calibrated at each test port using a set of three well-defined, precisely known reference impedances: a short circuit (0 ohms), an open circuit (infinite impedance), and a 50-ohm matched load - this "SOL" calibration lets the analyzer's error-correction math characterize and remove its own systematic measurement errors (directivity, source match, tracking) so that what's left is the true response of the device under test (correct answer B). The other choices either use impedances that aren't the real calibration standards (75/90 ohm, a "resonant circuit") or describe a completely different technique (lengths of cable) that isn't how VNA cal standards work.

question: How much power is being absorbed by the load when a directional power meter connected between a transmitter and a terminating load reads 100 watts forward power and 25 watts reflected power?
explanation: The power actually delivered to (absorbed by) the load is the forward power minus whatever was reflected back rather than absorbed: 100 W forward minus 25 W reflected = 75 W absorbed (correct answer D). This is simple power-balance bookkeeping for a directional wattmeter - the other answer choices (100, 125, or 112.5 W) don't correspond to any correct combination of the two readings.

question: What do the subscripts of S parameters represent?
answers: The port or ports at which measurements are made
explanation: In Smn notation, the two subscript digits identify the ports involved in that particular measurement: by convention the first digit is the port where the output/response is measured and the second digit is the port where the stimulus was injected (e.g., S21 = response measured at port 2 for a signal injected at port 1); when both digits are the same (S11, S22) it's a reflection measurement made entirely at that one port (correct answer A). The subscripts have nothing to do with measurement timing, data quality, or frequency ordering, so B, C, and D are wrong.

question: Which of the following can be used to determine the Q of a series-tuned circuit?
answers: The ratio of inductive reactance to capacitive reactance
The bandwidth of the circuit's frequency response
The resonant frequency of the circuit
explanation: A practical way to determine a tuned circuit's Q from a frequency-response sweep is Q = f0 / BW, where f0 is the resonant (center) frequency and BW is the -3 dB (half-power) bandwidth of the response curve - so measuring that bandwidth (with f0 known) directly yields Q (correct answer C). At resonance, XL always equals XC by definition, so their ratio is always 1 regardless of Q and reveals nothing about it, and knowing only the resonant frequency or the frequency shift, without the associated bandwidth, likewise doesn't determine Q, which rules out A, B, and D.

question: Which of the following can be measured by a two-port vector network analyzer?
explanation: A two-port VNA stimulates a device under test with a swept RF source and measures both the transmitted and reflected response versus frequency - exactly the technique used to characterize a filter's frequency response (its passband, insertion loss, and roll-off shape) (correct answer B). Phase noise is a spectral-purity property of an oscillator (measured with a phase-noise analyzer or spectrum analyzer, not a standard swept S-parameter VNA measurement), pulse rise time is a time-domain oscilloscope measurement, and forward power is simply read from a wattmeter - none of those are what a VNA's frequency-domain sweep is built to do.

question: Which of the following methods measures intermodulation distortion in an SSB transmitter?
answers: Modulate the transmitter using two RF signals having non-harmonically related frequencies and observe the RF output with a spectrum analyzer
Modulate the transmitter using two AF signals having non-harmonically related frequencies and observe the RF output with a spectrum analyzer
Modulate the transmitter using two AF signals having harmonically related frequencies and observe the RF output with a peak reading wattmeter
Modulate the transmitter using two RF signals having harmonically related frequencies and observe the RF output with a logic analyzer
explanation: The standard two-tone IMD test for an SSB transmitter feeds its microphone/audio input with two audio-frequency (AF) tones chosen to be non-harmonically related (e.g., roughly 700 Hz and 1900 Hz, deliberately not simple multiples of each other), then examines the resulting RF output on a spectrum analyzer; because the transmitter's audio processing and RF amplifier chain are what's under test, using AF tones (not RF tones) at its actual input is essential, and choosing non-harmonic tones keeps the unwanted third-order (and higher) IMD products from landing right on top of the tones' own harmonics, so they show up as clearly separate, measurable peaks (correct answer B). Modulating with RF signals instead of audio (A, D) doesn't exercise the transmitter the way it's actually driven in normal use, and using harmonically related tones (C) would mask the IMD products under the harmonics, defeating the test.

question: Which of the following can be measured with a vector network analyzer?
explanation: A VNA's fundamental output is the full set of S-parameters for a device, and input impedance, output impedance, and the reflection coefficient are all directly derived from (or are simply another way of expressing) those S-parameters - S11 and S22 are essentially the input and output reflection coefficients, which in turn convert directly to complex input/output impedance - so all three listed quantities are genuinely measurable with a VNA, making D ("all of these") correct.

question: What is an effect of excessive phase noise in an SDR receiver’s master clock oscillator?
answers: It limits the receiver’s ability to receive strong signals
It can affect the receiver’s frequency calibration
It decreases the receiver’s third-order intercept point
It can combine with strong signals on nearby frequencies to generate interference
explanation: A receiver's master (reference/sampling) clock isn't perfectly pure - it has phase noise, meaning its energy is smeared slightly into frequencies near the nominal clock frequency rather than concentrated at a single point. When a strong nearby signal is present, that smeared clock noise mixes with it during the receiver's frequency-conversion/sampling process (the same underlying mechanism as reciprocal mixing, see E4C13) and raises the effective noise floor right under the weak signal you're trying to copy, generating interference that wouldn't otherwise be there (correct answer D). This is a different, more specific effect than simply limiting strong-signal handling (A), degrading third-order intercept (C), or calibration drift (B) - phase noise's dominant practical symptom in an SDR is exactly this reciprocal-mixing-style interference from strong nearby signals.

question: Which of the following receiver circuits can be effective in eliminating interference from strong out-of-band signals?
explanation: A front-end (RF) filter or preselector, placed ahead of the mixer and first active gain stage, physically keeps strong out-of-band signal energy from ever reaching stages that could be overloaded or driven into intermodulation - which directly addresses interference caused by strong signals outside the band of interest (correct answer A). A narrow IF filter (B) only helps after the signal has already been converted and mixed with everything else in the receiver's passband; a notch filter (C) removes one specific in-band tone, not broadband out-of-band energy; and a product detector (D) is a demodulator stage that has nothing to do with keeping unwanted signals out.

question: What is the term for the suppression in an FM receiver of one signal by another stronger signal on the same frequency?
explanation: This is "capture effect" (correct answer C): because an FM demodulator only responds to frequency/phase deviation, not amplitude, when two FM signals share the same channel the demodulator locks onto and reproduces whichever one is even modestly stronger, effectively suppressing the weaker one - a threshold behavior unique to FM (unlike AM, where both signals would simply blend together audibly). Desensitization (A) is a different phenomenon involving a strong signal on a nearby, not the same, frequency reducing sensitivity, and cross-modulation (B) is the transfer of one signal's modulation onto another carrier via nonlinearity, not co-channel suppression - so A and B are wrong, and "frequency discrimination" (D) isn't a recognized term for this effect.

question: What is the noise figure of a receiver?
answers: The ratio of atmospheric noise to phase noise
The ratio of the noise bandwidth in hertz to the theoretical bandwidth of a resistive network
The ratio in dB of the noise generated in the receiver to atmospheric noise
The ratio in dB of the noise generated by the receiver to the theoretical minimum noise
explanation: Noise figure quantifies, in dB, how much additional noise a real receiver adds on top of the theoretical minimum (purely thermal) noise floor that a perfect, noiseless receiver would have at a standard reference temperature - the smaller the noise figure, the closer the receiver comes to that theoretical ideal (correct answer D). It is not a comparison to atmospheric or band noise (A, C - those depend on band and time of day, not receiver design) and choice B garbles the concept into an unrelated bandwidth-ratio statement, so A, B, and C are wrong.

question: What does a receiver noise floor of -174 dBm represent?
answers: The receiver noise is 6 dB above the theoretical minimum
The theoretical noise in a 1 Hz bandwidth at the input of a perfect receiver at room temperature
The noise figure of a 1 Hz bandwidth receiver
The receiver noise is 3 dB above theoretical minimum
explanation: -174 dBm is the well-known thermal noise power (kTB) available in a 1 Hz bandwidth from a perfect (0 dB noise figure) receiver at standard room temperature (290 K); computed from Boltzmann's constant (k ≈ 1.38x10⁻²³ J/K), kT ≈ 4x10⁻²¹ watts in 1 Hz, which works out to about -174 dBm (correct answer B). It's a theoretical reference point, not a statement about how far some particular real receiver's noise sits above or below that minimum (which is what A and D describe, and what "noise figure" itself expresses - see E4C04), and choice C misapplies "noise figure" to a bandwidth rather than to a receiver's actual excess noise.

question: How much does increasing a receiver’s bandwidth from 50 Hz to 1,000 Hz increase the receiver’s noise floor?
explanation: Receiver noise power scales directly with bandwidth (a wider bandwidth simply admits more thermal noise), so the increase in the noise floor in dB is 10 x log10(new bandwidth / old bandwidth) = 10 x log10(1000 Hz / 50 Hz) = 10 x log10(20) ≈ 13.0 dB (correct answer D). The other choices (3, 5, or 10 dB) don't correspond to a 20:1 bandwidth ratio - 3 dB would be a 2:1 ratio and 10 dB would be a 10:1 ratio, for comparison.

question: What does the MDS of a receiver represent?
explanation: MDS stands for Minimum Discernible (or Detectable) Signal - the weakest input signal level a receiver can just barely distinguish from its own internal noise (typically defined at a specified SNR, often around 0 to 3 dB, in a stated bandwidth) (correct answer B). The other expansions of the acronym in A, C, and D are invented and don't correspond to any real, standard receiver specification.

question: An SDR receiver is overloaded when input signals exceed what level?
answers: One-half of the maximum sample rate
One-half of the maximum sampling buffer size
The maximum count value of the analog-to-digital converter
The reference voltage of the analog-to-digital converter
explanation: In an SDR, the RF signal (after any front-end gain/filtering) is converted to digital samples by an analog-to-digital converter, which can only represent voltages within its fixed reference voltage range; once an input signal's instantaneous voltage swing exceeds that ADC reference voltage, the converter clips (saturates) and can no longer accurately represent the waveform, which is the defining overload point for an SDR receiver (correct answer D). This is a hard, digital clipping limit tied to the converter's voltage reference, not a function of sample rate, buffer size, or the ADC's maximum numeric count value in the way A, B, and C describe.

question: Which of the following choices is a good reason for selecting a high IF for a superheterodyne HF or VHF communications receiver?
answers: Easier for front-end circuitry to eliminate image responses
explanation: In a superheterodyne receiver, the unwanted "image" frequency sits exactly 2x the IF away from the desired frequency (on the opposite side of the local oscillator); choosing a higher IF pushes that image far from the desired signal, so a comparatively gentle, realistic front-end (preselector) filter can adequately reject it before the mixer - a low IF crowds the image close to the wanted frequency and would require an impractically sharp front-end filter to keep it out (correct answer C). Reduced drift, fewer components, and improved noise figure aren't inherent benefits of picking a high vs. low IF, so A, B, and D are wrong.

question: What is an advantage of having a variety of receiver bandwidths from which to select?
answers: The noise figure of the RF amplifier can be adjusted to match the modulation type, thus increasing receiver sensitivity
Receiver power consumption can be reduced when wider bandwidth is not required
Receive bandwidth can be set to match the modulation bandwidth, maximizing signal-to-noise ratio and minimizing interference
Multiple frequencies can be received simultaneously if desired
explanation: Matching the receiver's selected bandwidth to the actual bandwidth of the mode being received - narrow (e.g., ~500 Hz) for CW, wider (~2.4-3 kHz) for SSB voice, wider still for FM - admits only as much noise and adjacent-frequency energy as necessary to pass the wanted signal, which directly maximizes signal-to-noise ratio and minimizes interference from nearby signals that a too-wide filter would otherwise let through (correct answer C). It doesn't change the RF amplifier's noise figure (A), isn't primarily a power-saving feature (B), and doesn't enable receiving multiple frequencies at once (D).

question: Why does input attenuation reduce receiver overload on the lower frequency HF bands with little or no impact on signal-to-noise ratio?
answers: The attenuator has a low-pass filter to increase the strength of lower frequency signals
The attenuator has a noise filter to suppress interference
Signals are attenuated separately from the noise
Atmospheric noise is generally greater than internally generated noise even after attenuation
explanation: On the lower HF bands, atmospheric and man-made band noise picked up by the antenna (lightning static, galactic background noise, etc.) is typically far stronger than the receiver's own internally generated noise floor. Inserting attenuation ahead of the front end reduces both the desired signal and that atmospheric noise together by the same amount, but since the atmospheric noise - not the receiver's internal noise - was already the dominant limit on hearing weak signals, the effective signal-to-noise ratio barely changes, while the attenuation does reduce the risk of strong signals overloading front-end stages (correct answer D). The other choices describe mechanisms (selective low-pass filtering, separate attenuation of signal vs. noise) that don't reflect how a simple resistive attenuator actually works.

question: How does a narrow-band roofing filter affect receiver performance?
answers: It improves sensitivity by reducing front-end noise
It improves intelligibility by using low Q circuitry to reduce ringing
It improves blocking dynamic range by attenuating strong signals near the receive frequency
explanation: A roofing filter is a narrow bandpass filter placed immediately after the first mixer/IF conversion, ahead of the main IF gain chain and AGC, so it keeps strong signals that are near (but outside) the desired channel from ever reaching - and desensitizing or intermodulating in - the later high-gain IF stages; this directly improves blocking dynamic range (correct answer C). It isn't primarily a sensitivity/front-end-noise improvement (A) and doesn't itself address audio ringing from low-Q circuitry (B, which describes an unrelated, backwards idea - narrow filters actually tend to increase ringing, not reduce it via low Q), so D ("all of these") is wrong because A and B don't hold.

question: What is reciprocal mixing?
answers: Two out-of-band signals mixing to generate an in-band spurious signal
In-phase signals cancelling in a mixer resulting in loss of receiver sensitivity
Two digital signals combining from alternate time slots
Local oscillator phase noise mixing with adjacent strong signals to create interference to desired signals
explanation: Reciprocal mixing is what happens when a receiver's local oscillator has phase noise (energy smeared into frequencies near its nominal output) and a strong signal exists near, but not exactly on, the desired frequency: that LO phase noise mixes with the strong nearby signal during down-conversion and produces noise-like interference right on top of the desired (weaker) signal - interference that even a perfectly sharp IF filter can't remove, because it's generated in the mixing process itself, not from inadequate selectivity (correct answer D). The other choices describe unrelated effects (out-of-band signals combining into an in-band spur, in-phase cancellation, or digital time-slot mixing) that aren't what "reciprocal mixing" refers to.

question: What is the purpose of the receiver IF Shift control?
answers: To permit listening on a different frequency from the transmitting frequency
To reduce interference from stations transmitting on adjacent frequencies
To tune in stations slightly off frequency without changing the transmit frequency
explanation: The IF Shift control moves the receiver's IF passband relative to the fixed skirts of the IF filter (without changing the displayed or transmitted frequency), letting the operator slide an interfering signal near the edge of the passband off toward the filter's steep rejection slope while the desired signal, positioned differently within the passband, is retained with less attenuation - this reduces interference from adjacent-frequency stations (correct answer C). This is a distinct control from RIT/Clarifier, which is what choice D actually describes (shifting only the receive frequency, leaving the transmit frequency fixed) - a classic point of confusion on this exam, so D is a plausible-sounding but incorrect answer for "IF Shift" specifically.

question: What is meant by the blocking dynamic range of a receiver?
answers: The difference in dB between the noise floor and the level of an incoming signal that will cause 1 dB of gain compression
The minimum difference in dB between the levels of two FM signals that will cause one signal to block the other
The difference in dB between the noise floor and the third-order intercept point
The minimum difference in dB between two signals which produce third-order intermodulation products greater than the noise floor
explanation: Blocking dynamic range is defined as the difference, in dB, between the receiver's noise floor and the level of an interfering (undesired) signal that causes the receiver's gain to compress by 1 dB - a single-signal gain-compression spec, independent of any intermodulation product (correct answer A). Choice D actually describes a different, IMD-based dynamic range specification (often called "spurious-free" or "two-tone IMD" dynamic range), and B and C describe related-sounding but distinct or incorrectly framed concepts, so only A matches the standard definition of blocking dynamic range.

question: Which of the following describes problems caused by poor dynamic range in a receiver?
answers: Spurious signals caused by cross modulation and desensitization from strong adjacent signals
Oscillator instability requiring frequent retuning and loss of ability to recover the opposite sideband
